rows: Deliberate work with biological agents requires a COSHH risk assessment.
Biological agents should be classified by their hazard group.
Agent classification informs but does not replace assessment of the specific activity.
Laboratories and production facilities need containment measures appropriate to the work.
Risk assessment should consider workers with reduced immunity and new or expectant mothers.
Safe systems should address spills, disinfection and contaminated waste.
Exposure incidents may require medical referral and emergency response.
Notification or licensing can be required for specified agents or activities.
A hazard-group classification does not prove that a particular procedure is adequately contained.
Procedure conclusions require agent, concentration, method, containment, workers, waste, incident and notification evidence.
Blood-contaminated sharps can transmit serious bloodborne infections.
Work involving sharps should be risk assessed.
Safer sharp devices should be considered where they can reduce injury risk.
Needles should not be bent or forced during handling.
Used sharps should be disposed of promptly in suitable sharps containers.
Needles should not normally be re-used, re-sheathed or re-capped.
Workers need training in handling, disposal and response to sharps injuries.
Exposure incidents require prompt first aid, reporting and clinical assessment.
A sharps bin or safety needle does not prove the full work process is controlled.
Task conclusions require device, procedure, handling, disposal, worker, training, incident response and exposure evidence.
Work-related skin disease can be caused or worsened by chemical, biological and physical exposures.
Repeated wet work can damage the skin barrier.
Dermatitis is the most common work-related skin problem.
Employers should avoid harmful skin contact where practicable.
Protective measures should be selected for the substance and task.
Workers should check their skin for early signs of disease.
Training should explain skin hazards, hygiene and correct glove use.
Suspected work-related skin disease should prompt review of controls and suitable health advice.
A rash or glove-use record does not establish the cause or adequacy of control.
Individual conclusions require exposure, timing, skin distribution, products, wet work, controls and clinical evidence.
Employers must assess inhalation risks from respiratory sensitisers and other hazardous substances.
Substitution with a less harmful product should be considered.
Engineering controls such as local exhaust ventilation should be maintained in effective condition.
Administrative controls and supervision should support engineering controls.
Workers must follow the control measures and instructions provided.
Suitable health surveillance is needed for workers exposed or likely to be exposed to asthmagens.
Early symptoms should trigger occupational-health assessment and control review.
Reportable occupational-asthma cases should be handled through the applicable reporting process.
A product label or breathing complaint does not prove occupational asthma or exposure level.
Conclusions require agent, task, exposure route, controls, symptoms, timing, surveillance and clinical evidence.
